summary: Defines new states and status tags for the IETF Datatracker so working group chairs can show the progress of working group Internet-Drafts. It is informational.

eli5.summary: Stickers on a document pile showing each paper's stage, so everyone can see how far along it is.

questions: what are ietf working group document states
how does datatracker track draft status
what does it mean when a draft is adopted by a wg
subtitle: Tracking the progress of working group Internet-Drafts in the IETF Datatracker.

tldr.problem: The IETF Datatracker had no way to show working group chairs how their documents were progressing before submission to the IESG, only basic availability states like Active or Expired.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines new states (like 'Adopted by a WG', 'In WG Last Call', 'WG Consensus: Waiting for Writeup') and status annotation tags (like 'Awaiting Expert Review' or 'Author Needed') that chairs can apply to their drafts.
tldr.outcome: Working group chairs and delegates can now track and communicate the real status of documents through the lifecycle of WG development, making progress visible to all IETF participants.

facts.label: New working group states
facts.value: 10 main states from 'Call for Adoption' to 'Submitted to IESG'

facts.label: Intended maturity levels
facts.value: 7 levels: Experimental, Informational, BCP, Proposed, Draft, Standard, Historic

facts.label: Document type
facts.value: Informational; applies to IETF process only

today: RFC 6174 is an Internet Standard informational document that has not been obsoleted. The IETF Datatracker has been enhanced to implement the working group document states and annotation tags defined here, allowing chairs to provide better status tracking and visibility into the progress of working group drafts.

sections.title: The Tracking Problem
sections.content:
The IETF Datatracker is a web tool that manages Internet-Drafts, RFCs, and other aspects of the IETF process. It could already track documents that had been submitted to the IESG for publication, showing detailed states like 'In Last Call' or 'Approved'. However, the Datatracker had almost no way to show the status of documents while they were still being developed by a working group. It could only say whether a draft was 'Active' or had 'Expired', without explaining whether the group had actually adopted it or what stage of development it was in.

This made it hard for working group chairs to give meaningful status updates to participants, and impossible to see at a glance whether a draft was being actively worked on, waiting for input, or abandoned.
sections.eli5: Before this RFC, there was only a vague label like 'Active' for a draft. You could not tell if the group was seriously considering it, if it was being written, or if it was stuck.

sections.title: The Working Group I-D States
sections.content:
RFC 6174 defines a state machine for working group Internet-Drafts, beginning with 'Call for Adoption by WG Issued' (the group is considering the draft) and progressing through states like 'Adopted by a WG' (the group has agreed to own it), 'WG Document' (actively being developed), and eventually 'Submitted to IESG for Publication' (sent forward for approval).

Along the way, a document can move to 'In WG Last Call' (the group is doing a final review) or 'WG Consensus: Waiting for Writeup' (everyone agrees it is ready, but documentation work is pending). The state machine also includes 'Parked WG Document' (stalled for some reason) and 'Dead WG Document' (abandoned, though a dead draft can sometimes be revived). Unlike the IESG states that an Area Director assigns, these WG states are set by the group's chairs or their delegates.
sections.eli5: The states are like labels on a shelf: 'Being considered', 'We are working on this', 'Almost done', 'Sent for approval', or 'This one is stuck'.

sections.title: Status Annotation Tags
sections.content:
Beyond the main state, the RFC defines annotation tags that describe why a document is in a particular state or what is blocking progress. A draft can be tagged 'Awaiting Expert Review' to show that external technical review is happening, or 'Author or Editor Needed' to indicate that someone essential has left the document. Other tags include 'Waiting for Referenced Document' (the draft depends on another one that is not ready), 'Revised I-D Needed - Issue raised by WGLC' (the group found problems during last call that must be fixed), and 'Doc Shepherd Followup Underway' (the person writing up the document is working on it).

Multiple tags can be applied to a single draft, and they do not change the main state. They simply provide more detail about what is happening. A tag can be removed once the condition it describes is resolved.
sections.eli5: Tags are sticky notes: 'Waiting for expert opinion', 'We need a new author', 'The other document is not ready yet'. One draft can have several sticky notes at once.

sections.title: Integration with IESG States
sections.content:
The RFC explains how the new working group states sit in front of the existing IESG states. When a working group submits a draft to the IESG, the draft enters the IESG state machine (starting with 'Publication Requested' or 'AD Evaluation'). While the IESG is reviewing the document, the working group state remains 'Submitted to IESG for Publication'.

If an Area Director or the IESG sends the draft back to the working group for revision, the working group chair can move it back to an earlier state like 'WG Document' to indicate that active development is resuming. The Datatracker will automatically move a draft to 'Submitted to IESG for Publication' when publication is formally requested, and automatically move version-00 drafts to 'WG Document' when a chair approves them for posting.
sections.eli5: The WG states and IESG states are like two conveyor belts: the group uses its own labels until handing the draft to the IESG, then the IESG uses its own labels.

sections.title: Flexibility and Maturity Levels
sections.content:
The RFC emphasizes that working group chairs do not have to use all the states. Chairs may use whichever states make sense for their workflow. A chair might skip 'Parked WG Document' if nothing in the group is stalled, or might not conduct a Working Group Last Call at all (which is optional under IETF procedure).

Each working group draft must eventually have an 'intended maturity level' assigned before submission to the IESG: Experimental, Informational, Best Current Practice, Proposed Standard, Draft Standard, Standard, or Historic. The RFC notes that the Datatracker may need enhancements to let chairs set and change the intended maturity level. The states defined in this document provide no security implications, as they are purely administrative tracking within the IETF process.
sections.eli5: Groups are not forced to use every label. They pick the ones that help them keep track. Before sending a draft to the IESG, they must decide whether it will be for guidance, experimental practice, or a standard protocol.
